boilerplate.section_intro: This section consists of questions and problems involving quantitative reasoning.  Each question is followed by four possible responses.  Choose the correct answer and mark its number in the appropriate place on the answer sheet.

boilerplate.general_comments_title: General Comments about the Quantitative Reasoning Section
general_comments: The figures accompanying some of the problems are provided to help solve the problems, but are not necessarily drawn to scale.  Therefore, do not rely on the figures alone to deduce line length, angle size, and so forth.
If a line in a figure appears to be straight, you may assume that it is in fact a straight line.
When a geometric term (side, radius, area, volume, etc.) appears in a problem, it refers to a term whose value is greater than 0, unless stated otherwise.
When \(\sqrt{a}\) (a > 0) appears in a problem, it refers to the positive root of a.
"0" is neither a positive nor a negative number.

clusters.intro: Study the graph below, then answer the four questions that follow. A farmer examined the effect of a fertilizer on his lemon orchard. He divided the orchard into two equal plots: one plot he fertilized, and the other plot remained without fertilizer. At the end of each week the farmer examined the lemons that were picked in that week, and summarized in the graph four different measures for the lemons from each plot: average weight, average sugar content, average acidity level, and the number of lemons that were picked. The triangles in the graph indicate the values of each one of the four measures as a percentage of their value in week zero, which is the week before the division of the orchard, and they are connected by auxiliary lines (see key). When a measure stands at 100% its value is identical to its value in week zero. The farmer also compared, at the end of each week, the profits of the two plots in that week. He marked in the graph with ($) the profits from the sale of the fertilized lemons as a percentage of the profits from the sale of the unfertilized lemons. For example: At the end of week B the number of lemons that were picked in the fertilized plot was identical to the number of lemons that were picked in its area in week zero. The average sugar content in the unfertilized plot was 107.5% of its value in week zero. In that same week the profits of the fertilized plot were 92.5% of the profits of the unfertilized plot.

Study the graph and the table below, then answer the five questions that follow.

In a nature reserve live five species of animals: lions, zebras, leopards, rabbits and jackals.  On a certain day researchers conducted a study in the reserve and collected several kinds of data regarding the animals.
The graph describes the reserve, and marked in it are the areas in which the individuals of each species roamed on the day of the study (see key).  There can be overlap between the roaming areas of the species.  The black area in the centre of the graph marks a lake.
In the table beneath the graph additional data are presented that were collected on each species on the day of the study: the number of individuals of that species, the average weight of an individual (in kg), and the size of the roaming area in which the individuals stayed (in km²).  In addition, the table presents the diet of each species (regardless of the day of the study).

For example: On the day of the study the size of the roaming area of the lions was 48 km².  In one part of this area zebras also roamed, and in another part of this area jackals also roamed.  On the day of the study there were 10 lions in the reserve, and the average weight of a lion was 250 kg.

questions.stem: Over the course of the seven days of a certain week Gili made 29 telephone calls altogether. It is known that on Monday Gili made more telephone calls than on any other day in that same week. Therefore, on Monday Gili made at least ______ telephone calls.
Three of the following expressions are equal to one another. Which expression is different from the other expressions in its value?

methods.text: Put each under one root: \(\sqrt{12}\sqrt{15} = \sqrt{180}\), \(2\sqrt{45} = \sqrt{180}\), \(3\sqrt{30} = \sqrt{270}\), \(\sqrt{10}\sqrt{18} = \sqrt{180}\). The odd one is \(3\sqrt{30}\).
Moving a coefficient inside a root squares it. Three of the options were built to land on the same number, so converting to a single root is the only comparison needed.
Factor each bracket first: \(8x+2y = 2(4x+y)\) and \(16x-4y = 4(4x-y)\). The product is \(8(4x+y)(4x-y) = 8\left(16x^2-y^2\right)\).
Take \(x=1, y=1\): the product is \(10 \times 12 = 120\), and option (4) gives \(8 \times 15 = 120\).

Sarit has a keychain in the shape of a cube with a chain dangling from one of its vertices.
She wants to colour each one of the 8 vertices of the cube red or yellow, such that there will not be two vertices located on the same edge that are coloured in the same colour.

In how many different ways can she do this?
In which measure, in week B, was the largest gap (in absolute value) between the percentages that were measured in the fertilized plot and the percentages that were measured in the unfertilized plot?

In which week was the average acidity level in the lemons of the entire orchard the highest? (Assume that in week zero the acidity level in the two plots was identical, and that each plot has an equal weight when calculating the acidity level in the lemons of the orchard)
What is the first week in which the fertilized plot was responsible for more than half of the profits of the entire orchard?

Given that in week zero the same number of lemons was picked in the two plots. In week A 1,800 lemons were picked in the fertilized plot of the orchard. How many lemons were picked in week A in the unfertilized plot?

A and B are digits between 1 and 9.

Given:
  AB
– BA
  ――
  27

A – B = ?

methods.text: \(\overline{AB} - \overline{BA} = (10A+B) - (10B+A) = 9(A-B)\). Setting that equal to 27 gives \(A - B = 3\) directly.
Reversing a two-digit number and subtracting always gives 9 times the digit difference. So any such question is answered by dividing by 9 — no search needed.
Recognise \(120\) as \(5!\). Then the expression is \(\dfrac{5!\cdot5!}{(6!)^2}=\left(\dfrac{5!}{6!}\right)^2\), and \(\dfrac{5!}{6!}=\dfrac16\), so the answer is \(\dfrac1{36}\).
Or expand downward: \(6!=6\cdot5!\), so \((6!)^2=36(5!)^2\). The numerator is \(120\cdot5!=5!\cdot5!\), so everything cancels except \(\dfrac1{36}\). Never multiply \(720\times720\).

questions.stem: The accompanying figure shows a parallelogram whose side lengths are x and y. Given: 0° < α < 90° If S is the area of the parallelogram, which of the following statements is necessarily true?

On her way to work in the morning Liat drove for 20 minutes at a speed of x kph and afterwards drove for another 20 minutes at a speed of \(\frac{x}{2}\) kph.  In the evening Liat returned along the same road at a constant speed of y kph, and her drive lasted exactly one hour.

\(\frac{x}{y} = ?\)

methods.text: Morning distance: \(\frac{x}{3} + \frac{x}{6} = \frac x2\) km, since 20 minutes is a third of an hour.
The evening drive covers the same road in one hour at \(y\), so \(y = \frac x2\) and \(\frac xy = 2\). Both journeys are the same distance — that is the equation.
Set \(x = 60\): 20 km then 10 km, so 30 km total, done in an hour means \(y = 30\), and \(\frac{60}{30} = 2\) ✓.

questions.stem:
The accompanying figure shows a regular hexagon inscribed in a rectangle whose short side length is x.

What is the perimeter of the hexagon?

Given:  |a + b| < a

Which of the following statements is necessarily true?

methods.text: An absolute value is never negative, so \(a>0\). Unfolding gives \(-a<a+b<a\), and subtracting \(a\) throughout leaves \(-2a<b<0\). So \(|b|<2a\).
The given says \(a+b\) sits within \(a\) of zero. Slide that band down by \(a\) and \(b\) runs from \(-2a\) to 0 — a band of width \(2a\), which is exactly what option (1) states.
\(a=2,\ b=-1\) satisfies the given and makes \(|a|>|b|\), killing (3). \(a=2,\ b=-3\) satisfies it too and makes \(|b|>|a|\), killing (4) — and between them they kill (2) as well.

questions.stem:
The average of Yonatan's scores on three exams – language, literature and history – is 77.
On the exams in language and in literature Yonatan received the same score, and on the exam in history he received a score \(1\frac{1}{2}\) times as high as this score.

What is the score that Yonatan received on the history exam?

methods.text: Expanding: \(2xy+2x^2 + y^2-2xy - 2x^2 = y^2\). Everything in \(x\) cancels, so \(y^2 = 16\) and, \(y\) being positive, \(y = 4\).
That \(x\) vanishes entirely is the point of the question — which is why options (1) and (2), both written in terms of \(x\), cannot be right whatever the arithmetic.

questions.stem:
Rivka has 101 identical coins.  She divided them equally among her 4 children, and the remainder she added to the share of the firstborn son Chaim.  Chaim divided the coins that he received equally among his 3 children, and the remainder he added to the share of his firstborn daughter Yael.

How many coins did Yael receive?

methods.text: Two rounds of division with remainder. \(101 = 4 \times 25 + 1\), so each child gets 25 and Chaim keeps the extra 1 — he holds 26.
Then \(26 = 3 \times 8 + 2\), so each grandchild gets 8 and Yael keeps the extra 2 — she holds 10. The pattern is: quotient to everyone, remainder to the firstborn, twice.

2 $ -6 = ?
Given: a < 10 5 < b D = a – b Which of the following inequalities describes exactly the range in which D can be found?

methods.text: Never subtract one inequality from another. Flip \(5<b\) into \(-b<-5\), then add \(a<10\): \(D=a-b<5\).

\(D\) is largest when \(a\) is as large as possible and \(b\) as small as possible — just under 10 and just over 5, giving just under 5. And there is no lower bound at all, since \(a\) can be as negative as you like.
Options (1) and (2) give lower bounds, which the data cannot support. Between the two upper bounds, \(D=4\) is reachable (take \(a=9.9,\ b=5.9\)) so 2 is too tight.

4 machines of type A finish a job in 9 hours. 9 machines of type B finish the same job in 4 hours. \(\dfrac{\text{the time required for a machine of type A to finish the job alone}}{\text{the time required for a machine of type B to finish the job alone}} = ?\)

methods.text: Four A-machines take 9 hours, so one takes 36. Nine B-machines take 4 hours, so one takes 36 as well.
The ratio is 1. The numbers are swapped deliberately: \(4 \times 9 = 9 \times 4\), so the two jobs cost identical machine-hours and the individual machines are identical.

questions.stem:
In a pack of pencils there are 12 new pencils.  The length of a new pencil is 20 cm.
In each hour of writing Matan sharpens his pencil and shortens it by one centimetre.
Matan stops using a pencil when its length reaches 4 cm.

Assuming that Matan writes with a pencil 6 hours every day,
for how many days will a pack of pencils last him?

methods.text: Each pencil gives \(20 - 4 = 16\) usable centimetres, and one centimetre is one hour, so 16 hours a pencil and 192 hours for the pack.
Divide by the daily writing time to get the number of days.

questions.stem: Dvir tosses 3 fair dice. What is the chance that the sum of the results will be 17 at least?

x is an integer greater than 1.

Which of the following statements is true regarding the expression \(\sqrt{x^2 - x}\) ?
options: It can be an integer, but not an even number
It can be an integer, but not an odd number
It can be an even integer and it can be an odd integer

methods.text: \(x^2 - x = x(x-1)\), the product of two consecutive integers. For \(x > 1\) that sits strictly between \((x-1)^2\) and \(x^2\), so it can never be a perfect square.

Two consecutive integers are coprime, so for their product to be a square each would have to be a square itself — and no two consecutive positive integers above 1 are both squares. Either argument closes it.

questions.stem: In shop A the price of a short shirt is 20 shekels, and the price of a long shirt is 40 shekels. In shop B the price of every shirt is x shekels. On a certain day the two shops received an identical sum of money from the sale of shirts. On that same day an identical number of shirts was sold in both of them. On this day 30% of the shirts that were sold in shop A were long. x = ?

methods.text: Equal numbers of shirts and equal takings: if \(n\) short and \(n\) long sold in A, takings are \(60n\) from \(2n\) shirts, so B's price is \(\frac{60n}{2n} = 30\). Adjust for the actual split given in the stem.
With four numeric options, substituting each into both conditions is the reliable route; the arithmetic is one multiplication per option.

questions.stem:
In the accompanying system of axes is rectangle ABCD whose sides are parallel to the axes.

Given:  AD = 2 · AB

Based on this information and the information in the figure,
which of the following possibilities could indicate the values of point C ?
x is divisible by 2 without a remainder. y is divisible by 4 without a remainder. Which of the following numbers is the largest number by which the sum (x + y) is necessarily divisible?

methods.text: \(y\) divisible by 4 is also divisible by 2, and \(x\) is divisible by 2 — so the sum is divisible by 2. Nothing stronger: the two 2s do not combine.
\(x = 2,\ y = 4\) gives 6, which is not divisible by 4 or 8, killing those options; and \(x=2,\ y=8\) gives 10, not divisible by 6. Only 2 survives.
